SOURCE: "Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization", Diederik P. Kingma and Jimmy Lei Ba, ICLR 2015 (arXiv:1412.6980v9, dated 30 Jan 2017). File: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/01-llm-fundamentals/sources/kingma-2014-adam.pdf

COVERAGE: Read all 41,301 of 41,301 chars, pages 1 to 15, including the convergence-proof appendix (pp. 12-15). I skimmed the references (pp. 10-11) only to trace origins. Nothing was skipped.

CLAIMS
- claim: Algorithm 1. β1 drives the first-moment EMA of g. β2 drives the second raw-moment EMA of g². Each moment is divided by (1−β^t) using its own β. The update is α·m̂/(√v̂+ε).
  number: α=0.001, β1=0.9, β2=0.999, ε=10^-8
  setup: The paper calls these "good default settings for the tested machine learning problems". All operations are element-wise.
  quote: "Good default settings for the tested machine learning problems are α = 0.001, β1 = 0.9,β2 = 0.999 andϵ = 10−8." / "mt←β1·mt−1 + (1−β1)·gt (Update biased ﬁrst moment estimate) vt←β2·vt−1 + (1−β2)·g2t (Update biased second raw moment estimate) ˆmt←mt/(1−βt1) ... ˆvt←vt/(1−βt2) ... θt←θt−1−α·ˆmt/(√ˆvt +ϵ)"
  where: p.2, Algorithm 1
- claim: An equivalent and more efficient ordering folds both bias corrections into the step size. Note that ε here is a different ε̂.
  number: none
  setup: Section 2
  quote: "αt =α· √ 1−βt2/(1−βt1) andθt←θt−1−αt·mt/(√vt + ˆϵ)."
  where: p.2
- claim: The step size is bounded and works like a trust region. The bound is α·(1−β1)/√(1−β2) only in the extreme sparse case. Otherwise it is α, and typically |Δt| ⪅ α.
  number: |Δt| ≤ α·(1−β1)/√(1−β2) or ≤ α
  setup: Assumes ε=0. The first bound applies only when the gradient was zero at every step except the current one.
  quote: "Assumingϵ = 0, the effective step taken in parameter space at timestept is ∆t =α·ˆmt/√ˆvt. The effective stepsize has two upper bounds:|∆t|≤ α· (1−β1)/√1−β2 in the case (1−β1) >√1−β2, and|∆t|≤ α otherwise." / "This can be understood as establishing a trust region around the current parameter value, beyond which the current gradient estimate does not provide sufﬁcient information."
  where: pp.2-3, Section 2.1
- claim: The paper calls m̂/√v̂ the "SNR". It falls toward 0 near an optimum, which gives automatic annealing. The update is invariant to rescaling the gradient.
  number: none
  setup: Section 2.1
  quote: "the SNR value typically becomes closer to 0 towards an optimum, leading to smaller effective steps in parameter space: a form of automatic annealing." / "(c·ˆmt)/(√c2·ˆvt) = ˆmt/√ˆvt"
  where: p.3
- claim: Bias-correction rationale. Starting the EMA at zero gives E[vt] = E[g²]·(1−β2^t) + ζ, so dividing by (1−β2^t) removes the bias. Without the correction, initial steps are much larger when β2 is near 1.
  number: none
  setup: Section 3. ζ=0 if the second moment is stationary.
  quote: "= E[g2t ]· (1−βt2) +ζ (4)" / "What is left is the term (1−βt2) which is caused by initializing the running average with zeros. In algorithm 1 we therefore divide by this term to correct the initialization bias." / "it is exactly this case of small β2 where a lack of initialisation bias correction would lead to initial steps that are much larger."
  where: p.3
- claim: Removing bias correction gives RMSProp with momentum. With β2 near 1 that leads to very large steps and often divergence.
  number: none
  setup: Section 5
  quote: "RMSProp also lacks a bias-correction term; this matters most in case of a value of β2 close to 1 (required in case of sparse gradients), since in that case not correcting the bias leads to very large stepsizes and often divergence, as we also empirically demonstrate in section 6.4."
  where: p.5
- claim: VAE ablation (Fig. 4). Without bias correction, β2 near 1 was unstable, mostly in early epochs. The best results came from β2 near 1 with correction. Adam was equal to or better than RMSProp at every setting.
  number: β1∈[0,0.9]; β2∈{0.99,0.999,0.9999}; log10(α)∈[−5,−1]; 10 and 100 epochs
  setup: VAE as in Kingma & Welling 2013: one hidden layer of 500 softplus units and a 50-dim Gaussian latent.
  quote: "We iterated over a broad range of hyper-parameter choices, i.e. β1∈ [0, 0.9] and β2∈ [0.99, 0.999, 0.9999], and log10(α)∈ [−5,...,−1]." / "valuesβ2 close to 1 indeed lead to instabilities in training when no bias correction term was present, especially at ﬁrst few epochs of the training. The best results were achieved with small values of (1−β2) and bias correction" / "Adam performed equal or better than RMSProp, regardless of hyper-parameter setting."
  where: p.8, Section 6.4
- claim: Convergence. In the online convex setting the regret is O(√T) and average regret is O(1/√T). This requires αt=α/√t, β1,t=β1λ^(t−1) decaying, bounded gradients, a bounded parameter distance, and β1²/√β2<1.
  number: O(√T); λ e.g. 1−10^-8
  setup: Zinkevich 2003 online convex framework (Section 4, Theorem 4.1, Corollary 4.2)
  quote: "We show Adam hasO(√T ) regret bound" / "theorem holds when the learning rate αt is decaying at a rate of t− 12 and ﬁrst moment running average coefﬁcientβ1,t decay exponentially withλ, that is typically close to 1, e.g. 1− 10−8." / "andβ1,β2∈ [0, 1) satisfy β21√β2 < 1. Let αt = α√t andβ1,t =β1λt−1" / "R(T ) T =O( 1√T )"
  where: p.4
- claim: With sparse features, adaptive methods such as Adam and AdaGrad can reach O(log d·√T), compared with O(√(dT)) for non-adaptive methods. Decaying β1,t is important to the proof.
  number: O(log d √T) vs O(√dT)
  setup: Sparse, bounded-gradient case (Duchi et al. 2011, sec. 1.2)
  quote: "the adaptive method, such as Adam and Adagrad, can achieveO(logd √ T ), an improvement overO( √ dT ) for the non-adaptive method. Decaying β1,t towards zero is impor- tant in our theoretical analysis"
  where: p.4
- claim: Logistic regression, MNIST. Adam converged about as fast as SGD with Nesterov momentum, and both beat AdaGrad. So Adam was tied here, not clearly best.
  number: minibatch 128; αt=α/√t
  setup: L2-regularised multiclass logistic regression on 784-dim pixels
  quote: "we found that the Adam yields similar convergence as SGD with momentum and both converge faster than Adagrad."
  where: p.5, Section 6.1, Fig. 1
- claim: Logistic regression on IMDB bag-of-words, a sparse task. Adam matched AdaGrad, and both beat SGD-Nesterov by a large margin. Adam tied AdaGrad rather than beating it.
  number: 10,000 BoW features; 50% dropout on features
  setup: Maas et al. 2011 IMDB
  quote: "Adagrad outperforms SGD with Nesterov momentum by a large margin both with and without dropout noise. Adam converges as fast as Adagrad."
  where: p.6
- claim: MLP on MNIST. With a deterministic loss, Adam beat SFO per iteration and in wall-clock time; SFO is 5-10x slower per iteration. With dropout, Adam converged better than AdaGrad, RMSProp, SGD-Nesterov and AdaDelta, and SFO failed to converge.
  number: 2×1000 ReLU hidden units; minibatch 128; SFO 5-10x slower
  setup: Non-convex, so the theory does not apply.
  quote: "Due to the cost of updating curvature information, SFO is 5-10x slower per iteration com- pared to Adam" / "SFO assumes deterministic subfunctions, and indeed failed to converge on cost functions with stochastic regularization." / "Adam shows better convergence than other methods."
  where: p.6, Section 6.2, Fig. 2
- claim: CNN on CIFAR-10. Adam and SGD-Nesterov both converged much faster than AdaGrad, and Adam's edge over SGD was only "marginal". v̂ shrank toward zero and was dominated by ε. The paper's argued benefit here is per-layer rate adaptation without manual tuning.
  number: c64-c64-c128-1000; 45 epochs; minibatch 128
  setup: Whitened input; dropout on the input and FC layers
  quote: "We notice the second moment estimateˆvt vanishes to zeros after a few epochs and is dominated by the ϵ in algorithm 1." / "Though Adam shows marginal improvement over SGD with momentum, it adapts learning rate scale for different layers instead of hand picking manually as in SGD."
  where: p.7, Section 6.3, Fig. 3
- claim: AdaMax, the L∞ variant, uses ut = max(β2·ut−1, |gt|). It needs no bias correction on u, and its step bound is simply |Δt| ≤ α.
  number: α=0.002, β1=0.9, β2=0.999
  setup: Section 7.1, Algorithm 2
  quote: "Good default settings for the tested machine learning problems are α = 0.002, β1 = 0.9 and β2 = 0.999." / "ut = max(β2·ut−1,|gt|) (12)" / "we don't need to correct for initialization bias in this case. Also note that the magnitude of parameter updates has a simpler bound with AdaMax than Adam, namely:|∆t|≤ α."
  where: p.9
- claim: Temporal averaging. A bias-corrected EMA of the parameters is proposed as an alternative to Polyak-Ruppert averaging, framed as helping generalisation. It is not tested.
  number: none
  setup: Section 7.2
  quote: "¯θt←β2· ¯θt−1 +(1−β2)θt, with ¯θ0 = 0. Initalization bias can again be corrected by the estimatorˆθt = ¯θt/(1−βt2)."
  where: p.9
- claim: AdaGrad is the limiting case of Adam with β1=0, infinitesimal (1−β2), and αt=α·t^-1/2. The correspondence breaks without bias correction.
  number: none
  setup: Section 5
  quote: "AdaGrad corresponds to aversion of Adam withβ1 = 0, inﬁnitesimal (1−β2) and a replacement ofα by an annealed version αt =α·t−1/2"
  where: p.5
- claim: Methodology. All optimisers start from the same initialisation, and each reports its best setting from a dense hyperparameter grid.
  number: none
  setup: Section 6
  quote: "The hyper-parameters, such as learning rate and momentum, are searched over a dense grid and the results are reported using the best hyper-parameter setting."
  where: p.5

LIMITS:
- The proof covers only convex online problems, and it needs decaying αt and β1,t, which differs from the constant defaults in Algorithm 1. The authors say so: "Although our convergence analysis does not apply to non-convex problems, we empirically found that Adam often outperforms other methods in such cases." (p.6)
- All plots show training cost. There is no test error or accuracy, so the paper makes no generalisation comparison. The temporal-averaging generalisation claim is unsupported.
- The experiments are small: MNIST, IMDB BoW, CIFAR-10 with a 3-conv-layer net, and a 1-layer VAE. There are no error bars or seed counts, and no wall-clock numbers except for SFO.
- Adam was not clearly best everywhere. It tied SGD-Nesterov on MNIST logistic regression, tied AdaGrad on IMDB, and was only "marginal" over SGD-Nesterov on CIFAR-10.
- In the CNN, v̂ collapsed to the ε level, so the adaptive part contributed little there.
- Weight decay appears only as an L2 term in the loss. There is no decoupled weight decay.
- Outside knowledge, not from this source, to verify before citing: later work (Reddi et al. 2018, AMSGrad) is generally reported to have found a flaw in this convergence proof. Decoupled weight decay (AdamW) also post-dates this paper.

BUILDS ON: AdaGrad (Duchi et al., 2011); RMSProp (Tieleman & Hinton, 2012; Graves, 2013); online convex regret framework (Zinkevich, 2003); natural gradient (Amari, 1998) and the diagonal-Fisher view (Pascanu & Bengio, 2013); momentum-decay finding (Sutskever et al., 2013); Polyak-Ruppert averaging (Polyak & Juditsky, 1992; Ruppert, 1988; Moulines & Bach, 2011). Compared against SFO (Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2014) and AdaDelta (Zeiler, 2012); vSGD (Schaul et al., 2012) is also mentioned.

CODE: Algorithm 1 (p.2) and Algorithm 2 (p.9). The lines are quoted verbatim in CLAIMS 1 and 14. The core loop is:
"mt←β1·mt−1 + (1−β1)·gt / vt←β2·vt−1 + (1−β2)·g2t / ˆmt←mt/(1−βt1) / ˆvt←vt/(1−βt2) / θt←θt−1−α·ˆmt/(√ˆvt +ϵ)"

FIGURES:
- Fig. 1, p.6: "Logistic regression training negative log likelihood on MNIST images and IMDB movie reviews with 10,000 bag-of-words (BoW) feature vectors." It shows that Adam's best case is a tie: with SGD-Nesterov on dense data and with AdaGrad on sparse data.
- Fig. 2, p.7: "Training of multilayer neural networks on MNIST images. (a) ... dropout ... (b) ... deterministic cost function. We compare with ... (SFO)". It shows one plot with five optimisers, all on a log-scale loss.
- Fig. 3, p.7: "Convolutional neural networks training cost. (left) ... first three epochs. (right) ... 45 epochs. CIFAR-10 with c64-c64-c128-1000". It shows AdaGrad's early lead fading. This is the best figure for "adaptive is not always better".
- Fig. 4, p.8: "Effect of bias-correction terms (red line) versus no bias correction terms (green line) after 10 epochs (left) and 100 epochs (right) on the loss ... VAE ... for different settings of stepsize α ... β1 and β2." This is the strongest candidate: one picture shows why bias correction matters when β2 is near 1.

PROBLEMS:
- Extraction is clean apart from flattened math: superscripts run inline ("βt1" means β1^t, "g2t" means g_t², "t− 12" means t^(-1/2)). pypdf warned that fontTools was missing, but the text came out readable.
- There are textual inconsistencies in the source itself:
  - Section 3 says "the exponential decay rateβ1 can (and should) be chosen" while deriving the β2 term. That looks like a typo for β2.
  - Section 3 also says sparse gradients need "a small value of β2", but Sections 5 and 6.4 say β2 close to 1, that is, small (1−β2).
  - Section 2 says "decay rates are small (i.e. theβs are close to 1)".
  - Quote these carefully.
- The proof's last line (p.15) ends with a denominator of "2αβ1(1−λ)2", while Theorem 4.1/10.5 states "2α(1−β1)(1−λ)2". This is an internal inconsistency.
- Fig. 2(b) has no extractable data in the text.
- No embedded instructions were found.
